A frieze is essentially a long, horizontal decorative band or strip. Think of it as a ribbon of decoration stretched across a surface — usually a wall or a building — that is meant to be looked at and admired. The word has two distinct meanings depending on the context: one in architecture and design, and one in textiles. The architectural meaning is far more common, so we'll spend the most time there.
Meaning 1: A Decorative Band on a Wall or Building

This is the most important and widely used meaning of the word.

Imagine you are looking at a grand old building, or even a beautifully decorated room. Near the top of the wall — just below the ceiling or roof line — you notice a wide, flat, horizontal strip running all the way around, decorated with carvings, paintings, or patterns. That strip is a frieze.

A frieze is not just a thin line or a border. It is a substantial band, wide enough to tell a story or display a scene, but it always runs horizontally and is always flat against the surface of a wall or a structure.

In Classical Architecture (The Precise Technical Meaning)

In formal architecture — especially the ancient Greek and Roman style that still influences buildings today — the frieze has a very specific, exact location. When you look at a classical building with tall columns (like the Parthenon in Athens, or the Lincoln Memorial in Washington), the structure resting horizontally on top of those columns is called the entablature. This entablature is made of exactly three stacked layers:

  1. The architrave — the plain, flat band at the very bottom, sitting directly on the column tops.
  2. The frieze — the middle band, which is the decorative one.
  3. The cornice — the projecting ledge at the very top that juts outward like a roof edge.

So in this strict technical sense, the frieze is the middle section of the three-part horizontal structure that sits on top of columns. It is sandwiched between the plain architrave below and the overhanging cornice above. This is its precise architectural address, so to speak.

This middle band is where the sculptor or artist went to work. In Greek temples, the frieze was often carved with elaborate scenes — battles, processions of people and horses, mythological stories. The most famous example in the world is the Parthenon Frieze (sometimes called the Elgin Marbles), a 160-metre long carved marble band that originally wrapped around the entire inner wall of the Parthenon, depicting a grand ceremonial procession. It is considered one of the supreme masterpieces of ancient art.

In Everyday and Interior Design (The Broader Meaning)

Outside of the strict classical sense, the word frieze is used much more loosely to describe any decorative horizontal band running along a wall, regardless of whether the building has columns or not.

For example:

  • In a dining room, you might have a strip of patterned wallpaper running along the wall just below the ceiling — this can be called a frieze.
  • In a museum, a painted band of figures running around the upper portion of the walls is a frieze.
  • In a child's bedroom, a row of illustrated animals painted in a strip near the ceiling is a frieze.

The key qualities that make something a frieze in this general sense are:

  • It is horizontal (runs left to right, not up and down).
  • It is long, stretching across a wall or around a room.
  • It sits near the top of the wall, typically.
  • It is decorative — it is there to be seen and to add beauty or tell a story.

The decoration on a frieze can take many forms: carved stone relief, painted scenes, geometric patterns, repeated motifs (a repeated pattern or design element), or even mosaic tiles.
Meaning 2: A Type of Heavy Woolen Cloth

This is a much less commonly encountered meaning today, but it is worth knowing so the word never catches you off guard.

A frieze can also refer to a type of thick, coarse, rough woolen fabric. It is a heavy cloth that was historically used to make warm outer garments like coats and cloaks. One side of this fabric has a raised, shaggy, rough surface called a nap — similar to the feel of felt or a very heavy blanket. This cloth was popular in medieval and early modern Europe, especially in colder regions like Ireland, where it was produced widely.

You are most likely to come across this meaning in historical writing, classic literature, or texts about traditional textile crafts. In modern everyday speech, this meaning is rarely used.
How to Tell Which Meaning Applies

Context will almost always make it obvious:

  • If someone is talking about a building, a wall, a room, architecture, art, or decoration → they mean the decorative horizontal band.
  • If someone is talking about fabric, cloth, clothing, or textiles → they mean the rough woolen material.
Summary (The Whole Word at a Glance)

A frieze is:

  1. (Architecture & Design — primary meaning) A long, horizontal decorative band on a wall or building, especially the middle section of the three-part structure resting on top of classical columns. It is often carved, painted, or patterned, and frequently tells a visual story. In a looser sense, any decorative strip running horizontally along the upper part of a wall, inside or outside a building.
  2. (Textiles — secondary meaning) A heavy, rough, shaggy woolen cloth used historically for warm outer garments.

When you see the word "frieze," picture that long, flat, story-filled ribbon of decoration wrapping around a great building, and you will almost always be exactly right.
